title: AI in your community
essentialQuestion: How can AI help a community, and what could go wrong?
learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and risks of AI tools for translation, farming and health, and explain why people must stay in charge.

warmUp.question: Where do you think AI could help people in a community?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: How does each tool help? What could go wrong? Who checks it?

cards.title: Three AI tools in the town of Sunvale

cases.name: Translation tool at the community centre
cases.body: It turns notices into several languages, so more neighbours can read them. It is very good in languages with lots of writing online. It makes more mistakes in a language with little writing online. A volunteer who speaks that language checks important notices.

cases.name: Leaf tool for farmers
cases.body: A farmer takes a photo of a leaf, and the tool guesses if the plant is sick. It works with no internet. It learned from the leaves of three crops, so it often guesses wrong for a crop it has never seen. When it is not sure, the farmers' group asks a plant expert.

cases.name: Eye photo helper at the clinic
cases.body: It looks at photos of the eye and marks the ones that may show a problem, so busy health workers know who to see first. It learned mostly from photos of people in other places, and nobody has tested it in Sunvale yet. It might miss some problems there. A health worker always checks it and talks to each patient.

activity.title: Help or risk?
activity.instructions: Put each sentence about the Sunvale tools into a group. There is no score. After you place one, you can see one possible answer and the reason.

items.text: The translation tool lets more neighbours read notices.
items.feedback: More people can read important news in a language they know.

items.text: The translation tool makes more mistakes in some languages.
items.feedback: A wrong notice could tell people the wrong thing.

items.text: The leaf tool works with no internet.
items.feedback: Farmers can use it in fields far from any signal.

items.text: A farmer trusts a wrong guess and pulls out healthy plants.
items.feedback: The tool guesses, and a guess can be wrong.

items.text: The eye helper shows busy health workers who to see first.
items.feedback: Health workers can reach the people who need them most sooner.

items.text: The eye helper learned from people in other places. It is not tested in Sunvale yet.
items.feedback: Until it is tested with people in Sunvale, nobody knows how well it works there. It might miss problems for people unlike the ones it learned from.

items.text: The clinic collects eye photos to make the helper better.
items.feedback: Any group can be right here. Local photos could help test the tool and make it fairer. But health photos are private, so people must agree first, and the photos must be kept safe.

items.text: A volunteer checks important translated notices.
items.feedback: A person who knows the language catches the tool's mistakes.

activity.saves: The group the learner chose for each sentence, with the lesson's other answers.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. Nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: AI can help where helpers are few
sections.text: In many places, there are not enough health workers or other experts for everyone who needs them. AI tools can sometimes help, as in the made-up town of Sunvale, where three tools help with notices, crops and eye checks. Here is a real example from Singapore. People with diabetes need regular eye checks, because the illness can harm their eyes. Researchers there built a tool called SELENA+, which looks at photos of the back of the eye and marks the ones an eye specialist should see. In 2017, they reported tests with photos from Singapore's eye checks and from people in other countries. It found most of the problems that trained checkers found, but the researchers said it still needed testing in real clinics.
sections.simpler: Many places do not have enough health workers or other experts. AI tools can sometimes help. In made-up Sunvale, three tools help with notices, plants and eyes. In Singapore, researchers built a real tool called SELENA+. People with diabetes need eye checks, because the illness can harm their eyes. SELENA+ marks eye photos that an eye doctor should see. In 2017, it was tested on photos from Singapore and elsewhere. It found most problems that people found. It still needed tests in real clinics.

sections.heading: Every tool has risks
sections.text: A tool that helps can also cause problems, so it is important to weigh the benefits against the risks. The Sunvale eye helper learned mostly from photos of people in other places. That does not make it a poor tool. But nobody has tested it in Sunvale, so it might miss some problems there. A tool must be tested with the people it will serve. Translation tools make more mistakes in languages with little writing online. A farmer who trusts a wrong guess might pull out healthy plants. Health photos are also private, so they must be kept safe.
sections.simpler: A tool that helps can also cause problems. So weigh the benefits and the risks. The eye helper learned from people in other places. That does not make it bad. But nobody has tested it in Sunvale. It might miss problems there. Tools must be tested with the people they help. Translation tools make more mistakes in some languages. A farmer could trust a wrong guess. Health photos are private and must be kept safe.

sections.heading: People must stay in charge
sections.text: Because AI tools can be wrong, people need to stay in charge of important decisions. In Sunvale, a volunteer who speaks the language checks important translated notices. A plant expert helps when the leaf tool isn't sure, and a health worker always checks the eye helper. The people of a community should also help to shape the tools they use. Before trusting any AI tool, ask three questions. Who does it help? Who might it leave out? Who checks its answers? For any health question, always ask a health worker, not a tool.
sections.simpler: AI tools can be wrong. So people must stay in charge of big decisions. In Sunvale, a volunteer checks notices. An expert and a health worker check the other tools. People in a community should help shape their tools. Ask three questions. Who does it help? Who might it leave out? Who checks it? For health questions, ask a health worker.

glossary.definition: A person who knows a lot about one subject.
glossary.example: A plant expert helps the farmers in Sunvale.

glossary.definition: To change words from one language into another.
glossary.example: The tool translates notices at the community centre.

glossary.definition: A good thing that helps someone.
glossary.example: One benefit of the leaf tool is that it works with no internet.

glossary.definition: The chance that something bad could happen.
glossary.example: One risk is that a farmer trusts a wrong guess.

glossary.definition: A group of people who live in the same place or share something.
glossary.example: The people of Sunvale are a community.

checks.question: Why might the eye helper miss problems in Sunvale?

options.text: It was not tested with people there
options.feedback: Yes. It learned mostly from photos of people in other places. That might be fine, but only a test in Sunvale can show it.

options.text: Sunvale has no eye problems at all
options.feedback: Not quite. Eye problems happen everywhere. Look at what the tool learned from.

options.text: The health workers forget to use it
options.feedback: Not quite. They use it and check it. Read the second section about testing.

checks.question: What makes the translation tool safer to use?

options.text: Using it for every single notice
options.feedback: Not quite. Using it more doesn't fix its mistakes. Read the third section.
Not quite. The tool is there to help people read. Read the third section.
Yes. A person who speaks the language can catch the tool's mistakes.

checks.question: Which Sunvale tool would help a community you know? What would worry you about it?
checks.placeholder: The ___ would help because ... I would worry that ...

write.prompt: Choose one Sunvale tool. Explain one way it helps, one risk, and who should check it.
selfCheck: I named one tool from Sunvale.
I gave one benefit and one risk.
I said who should check it.
write.example: I chose the leaf tool. It helps because farmers can find out quickly if a plant may be sick, even with no internet. One risk is that it gives a wrong guess for a crop it has never seen. This could happen because its training data only had leaves from three crops. A farmer who trusts a wrong guess might pull out healthy plants. A plant expert should check it when the tool is not sure, because people need to stay in charge.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner names a Sunvale tool. You say one way it helps and one risk. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud why a person should always check an AI tool that helps with health.

watch.title: Ethics & AI: Equal Access and Algorithmic Bias
watch.why: People who build and study AI talk about how AI can help everyone, or leave some people out.
watch.beforeQuestion: Who do you think should decide how an AI tool is used in a community?
watch.afterQuestion: Why does it matter who builds an AI tool?
watch.summary: In this video, people who build and study AI talk about fairness. AI tools learn from data, and they are already used in many parts of life. The speakers say AI could help more people get what they need. But AI can also be unfair. If the data, or the people who build a tool, leave some groups out, the tool can work worse for those groups or treat them unfairly. This is called algorithmic bias. The speakers say that people from many different backgrounds should help to build AI. They also say that people must keep checking AI tools, so that the tools help everyone and don't harm the people they leave out.
keyPoints: AI can help more people, or it can treat some people unfairly.
Unfair results often come from data or teams that leave some people out.
People from many backgrounds should help to build and check AI.
watch.contentNote: About 3 minutes 20 seconds. The speakers name the AI companies, car company, universities and groups they work for. The summary was written from DCMP's description of the video and its list of speakers, not from watching it. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Health: the Sunvale eye helper is made up; SELENA+ is real, and the lesson describes only how it was built and tested. Never give or discuss medical advice or diagnoses; learners with health questions should ask a health worker. Don't ask learners about their own health or anyone else's, including diabetes in their family.
Don't ask which languages learners speak at home, or which language a tool got wrong for them. Let them say so if they want to.
educatorNotes: The Sunvale tools are made up and stay labelled; SELENA+ is real and appears only in the reading, never in the made-up evidence or activity. What the sources establish: SNEC's page says SELENA+ was developed with about 500,000 retina photos and checked on 10 outside sets of photos (different cameras, ethnic groups and ages), and is approved by Singapore's health products regulator and CE-marked. The 2017 JAMA study tested it on 14,880 patients' photos from Singapore's national diabetic eye screening programme and on 10 other groups; it found referable eye disease with high sensitivity and specificity compared with trained graders, and said more research was needed for use in health care. The developers' own 2024 case study (Gunasekeran and others, NEJM AI) describes putting it into that programme; the lesson does not claim rollout or patient results, because no independent evaluation was checked. Other real projects, for teachers only: an offline cassava-disease phone app by IITA and Penn State (2018); WHO's 2021 report on AI for health; CLEAR Global's human checking of language technology.
Paper version of the activity: write the eight sentences on cards and sort them into Help, Risk and Both. The activity has no score; reward reasons.
